corrected_value.authors: Tian, J., Braithwaite, D. W., & Siegler, R. S.
corrected_value.title: Distributions of textbook tasks predict student learning: Data from decimal arithmetic.

decisions.location: Section 4 Discussion, lines 1779-1787; see also Section 2 Textbook Content Analyses (Study 1), lines 313-317, 386-404, 628-641, and References, lines 2248-2252
decisions.quote:
The analyses of decimal arithmetic problems in Swiss textbooks match Tian et al.’s findings

(2021) for U.S textbooks (see also Table 2), showing a nonrandom and unbalanced

distribution, too. For instance, in SZB only 12% and in MTB only 16% of addition and

subtraction problems involve decimals with unequal decimal digits, while 32% in SZB and

34% in MTB involve decimals with equal decimal digits.
decisions.reason: In Study 1 (Section 2, 'Textbook Content Analyses (Study 1)') and Section 4 ('Discussion'), Babari, Rütsche, & Schalk (10.23668/psycharchives.21850) explicitly re-test the empirical textbook distribution findings of both Braithwaite & Siegler (2018, 10.1037/xlm0000546, fraction arithmetic in U.S. textbooks, shipped row 456, target_index 0) and Tian, Braithwaite, & Siegler (2021, Journal of Educational Psychology 113(3):516-529, 10.1037/edu0000618, decimal arithmetic in U.S. textbooks, candidate target_index 1). Following Tian et al.'s (2021) coding scheme, the authors analyze 538 decimal arithmetic problems in the Swiss textbook series SZB and 766 decimal problems in MTB, compare their distributions directly against Tian et al.'s (2021) U.S. textbook data in Table 2 and Sections 2.2 and 4, and extend the behavioral test of those decimal textbook biases to Swiss students in Study 2. Tian et al. (2021) is a distinct empirical original paper (different first author, year, journal, and mathematical domain) that is empirically re-tested and absent from the shipped rows. Both listed prior adjudication/state files (d435618b...json and 5c674783...json) are absent.
